newsitem.title: UK: Irish premier chides Sinn Fein, urges IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Irish premier chides Sinn Fein, urges IRA truce.

text.p: BELFAST, May 30 - Irish Prime Minister John Bruton added his voice to U.S. and British pressure for an IRA truce on Friday, saying there was a place for Sinn Fein at the peace talks.

Bruton, a partner in an Anglo-Irish peace process, said republican demands for "clarification" were pointless because the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm knows its entry into the peace process is conditional on an to violence.
"There is a place for them. The truth of the matter is that they will be there if the IRA have a ceasefire and they know that," he told an Irish radio station.
"It is absolutely clear and there is no need for clarification that they will be in the talks," said Bruton, whose three-party coalition could face a tough re-election battle in a poll on Friday.
He was speaking after President Bill Clinton urged the Irish Republican Army on Thursday "to lay down their guns for good".
But a Sinn Fein leader said on Friday that it was concerned by Britain's refusal to give the assurances it has requested.

"We were disappointed this week that we didn't get the answers and we are perplexed and somewhat concerned that the British government representatives did not have answers to those questions," Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin told BBC radio.
He insisted his party was working urgently for an end to violence by all sides in the British-ruled province.
Multi-party talks are due to reopen in Belfast next Tuesday.
At a joint news conference with Britain's new Prime Minister Tony Blair in London, Clinton said the IRA could not talk and shoot at the same time.

The IRA, which has not staged any attacks in Northern Ireland since April 10, is pledged to wrench Northern Ireland from British control and merge it with neighbouring Catholic Ireland. The majority Protestants want to remain under London.
Sinn Fein insists that Britain guarantee it immediate entry to talks in the event of an IRA ceasefire, but London says proof of a genuine truce will be needed first.
The IRA accused the previous Conservative government of reneging on a deal for Sinn Fein's entry into the talks and ended a 17 month truce in February 1996 by exploding a massive bomb in London.
Blair, elected with a landslide win for his Labour Party on May 1, relaxed a ban on contacts with Sinn Fein that was imposed after the London blast.
He says he wants to gauge whether Sinn Fein and the IRA are genuine in saying they wish to resolve decades of Northern Ireland conflict by democratic methods.
Asked about the current political situation, McLaughlin said it was necessary that any cessation of violence was not derailed by unforeseen events.

"We are trying to anticipate difficulties and come up with solutions. We believe that that can done. I think as a matter of urgency...we do have considerable experience behind us now in terms of the peace process. The issues are well known and I think that we can arrive at definite conclusions and resolutions," he added.
